clinicalPearls: A benign monoclonal hepatocellular neoplasm classically seen in women taking oestrogen-containing contraceptives and in users of anabolic-androgenic steroids
Multiple adenomas (adenomatosis) and specific subtypes are associated with glycogen storage disease, obesity and the metabolic syndrome
The two principal clinical concerns are haemorrhage, especially with lesions larger than about 5 cm or those that are subcapsular, and malignant transformation to hepatocellular carcinoma
Molecular subtyping is central: inflammatory, HNF1-alpha-inactivated, beta-catenin-activated, and unclassified types differ in behaviour
Beta-catenin-activated adenomas carry the greatest risk of malignant transformation and are more common in men
MRI helps subtype the lesion, with HNF1-alpha adenomas showing diffuse fat and inflammatory adenomas showing the atoll sign and marked enhancement
First-line management is oral-contraceptive cessation and weight loss with interval imaging, reserving embolisation or resection for large, growing, symptomatic, male-sex or high-risk subtype lesions
reference.pathophysiology: Hepatocellular adenoma is a benign clonal proliferation of hepatocytes strongly influenced by sex-steroid hormones, arising against a background of oestrogen or androgen exposure and metabolic factors. Distinct genetic drivers define subtypes: HNF1-alpha inactivation produces steatotic adenomas, activation of inflammatory signalling pathways produces telangiectatic/inflammatory adenomas prone to bleeding, and beta-catenin activation predisposes to atypia and malignant transformation. The lesions are perfused by unpaired arteries without a normal ductal framework, and their thin-walled vasculature and lack of fibrous support underlie the tendency to rupture and haemorrhage.
additionalDifferentials: Focal fatty change or fat-containing lesion
additionalInvestigations: Multiphase contrast-enhanced MRI, ideally with a hepatobiliary agent, to characterise and subtype the lesion
Assessment of lesion size and subcapsular location to estimate bleeding risk
Liver function tests and, in adenomatosis, evaluation for glycogen storage disease
Alpha-fetoprotein and imaging surveillance to monitor for malignant transformation
Biopsy in selected cases to confirm subtype when management hinges on it
Hormonal and metabolic history including contraceptive, anabolic-steroid and metabolic-syndrome factors
redFlags: Acute severe abdominal pain with haemodynamic instability from ruptured adenoma and haemoperitoneum
Lesion larger than approximately 5 cm or demonstrable growth on follow-up
Beta-catenin-activated subtype or male sex, given elevated malignancy risk
Rising alpha-fetoprotein or imaging features suggesting transformation to carcinoma
reference.prognosis: Many small adenomas stabilise or regress after removal of hormonal drivers and weight loss, but larger or high-risk lesions carry risks of haemorrhage and malignant transformation, so selected cases require intervention and continued surveillance.
pitfalls: Mistaking an adenoma for focal nodular hyperplasia and underestimating bleeding and malignancy risk
Continuing oestrogen-containing contraception or anabolic steroids after diagnosis
Assuming a small lesion is safe without accounting for subtype and patient sex
Attempting biopsy of a highly vascular subcapsular lesion without weighing haemorrhage risk
Neglecting surveillance in patients managed conservatively
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of benign liver tumours
management: Withdraw hormonal drivers by stopping oestrogen-containing contraceptives and anabolic-androgenic steroids, and encourage weight loss, since many small adenomas then regress
Resect lesions that are large, subcapsular, enlarging, beta-catenin-activated, or occurring in men, given the risks of haemorrhage and malignant transformation
Manage acute intralesional or intraperitoneal haemorrhage with resuscitation and transarterial embolisation, followed by interval resection if needed
Surveil smaller lesions with serial contrast-enhanced MRI and alpha-fetoprotein for growth or malignant change
Counsel women on the risk of enlargement and rupture in pregnancy and plan accordingly
In adenomatosis, evaluate and manage associated glycogen storage disease and the metabolic syndrome
Refer to a hepatobiliary multidisciplinary team for decisions on resection versus surveillance
